title: TOP 15 Ancient Biblical Places That Actually Exist
fullText: Most of us grew up hearing these names the way we hear the names of castles in fairy tales. Jericho, Nineveh, Armageddon. Words that seem to belong to a book, not to a map. Places you could read about but never buy a bus ticket to. And then you find out you can. A shepherd throws a stone into a dark cave, hears something break, and changes what the world knows about its oldest book. A tunnel carved out of solid rock almost 3,000 years ago that you can still wade through today with the water up to your knees. A block of stone bearing the name of the man who sentenced Jesus to death found being used as a step in a staircase. And a mosque blown apart by extremists revealing a lost Assyrian palace hidden underneath it the whole time. These are 15 ancient biblical places [music] that actually exist that you can stand in right now. Before we start, do me a favor. Drop a comment telling us where you are watching from and what time it is right now. We want to see how far this one travels tonight. Let's begin. Number 15. The mountain where a man was shown everything he would never have. In Jordan, about half an hour west of the city of Madaba, a long ridge rises out of the desert and then simply stops. The land drops away and suddenly you are looking across the Jordan Valley over the pale glitter of the Dead Sea all the way to the hills of the West Bank. On a clear morning, people say you can make out Jericho and even the faint smudge of Jerusalem far beyond it. This is Mount Nebo. And according to Deuteronomy, this is where Moses was brought at the very end of his life. 40 years of wandering, 40 years of promising his people a land they had never seen. And here at the edge, he was shown all of it and told [music] he would not be going in. He died on this mountain and was buried somewhere nearby. And the text says plainly that no one knows the place of his burial to this day. The site is real and it is looked after by Franciscan friars who have excavated here since the 1930s. They uncovered the remains of a church built by early Christians who came here as pilgrims along with some of the most beautiful Byzantine floor mosaics in the region. Hunters and lions and a man leading an ostrich on a leash laid down more than 1,400 years ago. What stays with visitors is not the mosaics though. It is the view. You stand where the story says he stood and you see exactly what he saw [music] and you understand the shape of the ending without anyone having to explain it to you. Moses looked across at the Jordan River and stopped. Our next place is what waited on the other side of that water. Number 14. The holy site that was buried under landmines. For decades, one of the most significant sites in Christianity sat in a place where nobody was allowed to walk. Not because it was lost, because it was mined. On the eastern bank of the Jordan River in [music] the Kingdom of Jordan, there is an area the Bible calls Bethany beyond the Jordan. Described as the place where John was baptizing [music] and where Jesus came to him. After the wars of the 20th century, this stretch of riverbank became a military frontier. Barbed wire, watchtowers, minefields laid right across the ground where pilgrims had once come by the thousand. So for most of living memory, the site was not excavated, not visited, and not even approachable. It sat frozen a few hundred meters from a river, guarded by explosives. Then in 1994, Jordan and Israel signed a peace treaty. The demining began, and once the ground was declared safe, archaeologists walked in and started digging. What came out of the sand was remarkable. The remains [music] of churches stacked on top of each other. Baptismal pools cut into the earth. Stone steps leading down toward where the river once ran, worn smooth [music] by feet. A cluster of caves used by hermits who came out here to live alone in the desert. In 2015, the site was inscribed as [music] a UNESCO World Heritage location. The strangest detail is the river itself. The Jordan has shifted its course over the centuries, so the ancient baptism pools now sit some distance from the modern water. The pilgrims built at the water's edge. The water quietly walked away. That was a place preserved by accident [music] because nobody could reach it. Our next one preserves something far more embarrassing. Right out in the open. Number 13, the city that got insulted about its plumbing. In the book of Revelation, there is a line that has been quoted at people for 2,000 years. a message to the church at Leodysia telling them they are neither cold nor hot but lukewarm and that being lukewarm is worse than either. Most people hear that as a metaphor about faith. Stand in the ruins of Leodysia in southwestern Turkey and you start to suspect it was also a joke about the water. Leodysia was rich. It was a banking city, a center for textiles and eye medicine. And it sat in a valley with two famous neighbors. To the north, Heropoulos with its hot mineral springs that still pour out steaming white terraces you can see from kilome away. Nearby, cold, fresh mountain water. Leodysia had neither. It had to pipe its water in from a distance. And by the time that water arrived, it had lost its heat and picked up minerals along the way. You can see the evidence today. Sections of the old stone pipes have been excavated and the insides are thick with hard white calcium deposits narrowed by centuries of mineral buildup. The water arrived warm, heavy with minerals and unpleasant to drink. Scholars have argued this reading for a long time, and it is not the only interpretation on offer. But when you are standing in that valley looking at the steam rising off Heropolis on one side and the calcified pipes at your feet, it is very hard not to feel that the original audience heard something the rest of us have been missing. Not a gentle spiritual metaphor, a jab about their tap water that every single person in that city would have understood instantly. Leodysia was one of seven cities named in that book. Our next stop is another one of them and it holds the single most cinematic scene in the entire New Testament. Number 12, the theater where the riot happened. Ephesus on the western coast of Turkey is one of the best preserved ancient cities anywhere in the world. Marble streets still rutdded by cartwheels. The great facade of the library of Celsius. Public latrines with the seats still in place side by side. No partitions because privacy was somebody else's idea. But the thing you should walk to is the great theater cut into the hillside holding something in the region of 25,000 people. The book of Acts describes a scene here that reads like a film. A silver smith named Demetrius who makes silver shrines of the goddess Artemis realizes that the new preaching in the city is bad for business. Fewer people buying shrines. He gathers the other craftsmen and makes an argument that is refreshingly honest about its motives. That this is coming for their livelihood and also of course for the honor of the great goddess. The city erupts. A crowd drags [music] Paul's companions into the theater and then according to the account the mob starts chanting, "Great is [music] Artemis of the Ephesians over and over for about 2 hours. You can walk into that theater today and sit down on the stone. It has not moved. The acoustics still works so well that a person speaking at normal volume in the center can be heard high up in the seats. As for the goddess herself, the temple of Artemis was one of the seven wonders of the ancient world and it stood just outside the city. Go looking for it now and you will find a flat marshy field with a single reassembled column standing in it, usually with a stork nesting on top. 25,000 voices shouted for two hours that their goddess would never fall. The theater they shouted it in is still standing. The temple they were shouting about is a puddle and one column. Ephesus was excavated for over a century. Our next city has barely been touched at all. Number 11, the city nobody has dug up. There is a letter in the New Testament called the letter to the Colossians. It is addressed to a Christian community in a city called Colass in what is now Turkey. And people have been reading it and preaching from it for 2,000 years. The city itself is still there. You can drive to it and it is essentially a grassy hill. Colass sits under a large mound, what archaeologists call a Hoyuk in the Leis Valley, not far from Leodysia. Surveys have been carried out. Pottery has been collected from the surface, showing occupation going back thousands of years. Traces of a theater are visible in the slope. But compared to its famous neighbors, the site has never been through a full sustained excavation. For most of the modern era, it is simply sat there farmed around largely undisturbed. Which means that underneath that quiet hill, in theory, is the street layout of a city we have read about our entire lives. houses, public buildings, possibly the remains of the very community that letter was addressed to. Now, I can already hear some of you. If nobody has excavated it, does it really belong on a list of biblical places that actually exist? I would say yes, and I think it is one of the most interesting entries here precisely for that reason. Every other site on this list has been dug, cataloged, roped off, and photographed from every angle. This one is still sealed. Tell me in the comments whether you think that counts. From a city still waiting under the grass to a city that was violently dug into by exactly the wrong people. Number 10, the tomb that was destroyed and what it revealed. In Mosul in northern Iraq, there was a mosque known as Nabi Ununice, the mosque of the prophet Jonah. It stood on a hill on the eastern side of the Tigris and it was one of the most venerated sites in the city, honored by Muslims and Christians alike as the burial place of the prophet who in the story spent 3 days inside a great fish. In July of 2014, after seizing Mosul, militants of the Islamic State rigged the mosque with explosives and blew it up. Video of the destruction went around the world. It was by any measure an act of cultural eraser aimed at a shrine that had stood for centuries. But that hill was never just a mosque. Nabiunas sits directly on top of ancient Nineveh, the great Assyrian capital, the very city Jonah is sent to in the story. And because the mosque was there and because it was sacred, archaeologists had never been able to properly excavate beneath it. The militants had no such hesitation. They dug tunnels down under the ruins, hunting for antiquities to loot and sell. And when Iraqi forces retook the area in 2016 and 17, and archaeologists finally went down into those tunnels, they found themselves walking through the remains of an Assyrian palace. Carved reliefs, inscriptions naming kings, including Esser Hadon, chambers that had been sealed under that hill for more than 2 [music] and a half thousand years, exposed by lutters who were only interested in what they could carry out. The tunnels were unstable and crudely cut. Some of what was found had already been [music] damaged or stripped. Teams have worked since then to document and stabilize what remains. It is an ugly way for a discovery to happen. A shrine destroyed, a site looted, [music] and out of that damage, a lost palace suddenly visible for the first time in recorded history. Nobody who cares about that place would have chosen the trade. from a city buried under a hill to a village on a lake shore where the buildings are still standing. Number nine, the house at the center of everything. On the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee sits Capernium, a small fishing village that the gospels describe as the base of operations for most of Jesus's public work. It is mentioned again and again. He teaches here, heals here, calls fishermen from these boats. The village is real and much of it has been excavated. You can walk the black basalt foundations of first century houses, small rooms clustered around shared [music] courtyards, all built from the dark volcanic stone of the region. There is a beautiful white limestone synagogue standing in the middle of it, and almost every visitor assumes it is the synagogue from the gospels. It is not. That structure dates from several centuries later. But look at what is underneath it. [music] Beneath that white building, excavators found the black basaltt foundations of an earlier synagogue from a much older period. So the later builders put their synagogue directly on top of the previous one, which is exactly what communities tend to do. And a short walk away is the part that gets people quiet. Franciscan archaeologists excavated a modest first century house that was at some point singled out. Its main room was plastered, unusual for an ordinary home. Later it was enclosed by a church. Later still an octagonal church was built centered directly over that one room. Early visitors graffiti was found scratched into the plaster. Somebody very early on decided that this specific room in this specific house mattered enormously and generation after generation kept building around it rather than over it. The tradition identifies it as the house of Peter. The identification cannot be proven with certainty and honest archaeologists say so. What can be shown is that people were treating that room as sacred within a few generations which means someone in that village remembered something and did not want it forgotten. That was a place people fought to preserve. Our next one nobody had to preserve at all because it never stopped being used. Number eight, the well that has never gone dry. In the town of Nablas in the West Bank at the foot of Mount Garazim, there is a well. It is very old and very deep. Somewhere in the region of 40 m down, cut through rock. The Gospel of John describes a conversation at a well in this area between Jesus, tired from the road, and a Samaritan woman who came to draw water in the middle of the day. It is one of the longest recorded conversations [music] in the Gospels, and it happens over a bucket. What makes Jacob's well unusual among biblical sites is how little argument there is about it. Wells are not like buildings. Buildings get destroyed, moved, rebuilt, misremembered. [music] A well is a hole in the ground. You cannot relocate it and you cannot really fake it. [music] Its location has been pointed to consistently by Jewish, Samaritan, Christian, and Muslim tradition for a very long time. Churches have been built over it, destroyed, and built again. Crusaders raised one. Earthquakes and wars took them down. Today, the well sits in the crypt of a Greek Orthodox church under a low stone ceiling in the quiet. And here is the part that gets people. It still works. Visitors are handed a bucket on a rope. You lower it into the dark, wait, and hear it hit water far below. You crank it back up and drink. Every other site on this list asks you to imagine. This one hands you a cup of cold water from the same [music] source and lets you do what people did here 2,000 years ago without changing a single thing about the process. Now, if you are enjoying this, take one second and hit the like button. It tells the algorithm to show this video to more people who love places like these. And that is genuinely all it takes because from here on the certainty starts to fall apart. Number seven, the mountain that might be the wrong mountain. Everybody knows Mount Si. It is where in the book of Exodus, Moses climbs into the cloud and comes back down carrying the commandments. It might be the single most famous mountain in the western imagination. Nobody can agree on which mountain it is. The traditional identification is Jebel Musa in the south of the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt. And there is something extraordinary at its base. St. Catherine's Monastery, a fortified Orthodox monastery with walls built in the sixth century under the emperor Justinian and one of the oldest continuously operating monastic communities on earth. Inside there is a library [music] holding one of the most important collections of ancient manuscripts anywhere and a living bramble that the monks [music] maintain as the burning bush. Pilgrims have been climbing that mountain since at least the 4th century. There are around 3,700 steps cut into the rock by monks called the steps of repentance, and people still climb them in the dark to reach the summit at sunrise. But the identification comes from Christian tradition, largely settled in the early centuries [music] after Christ. It is not established by inscription and there is no archaeological find at the summit that ties the mountain to the Exodus account. So other candidates have been proposed. Jebel Serbal elsewhere in the Sinai Harcom in the Negv desert championed by the archaeologist Emanuel Anadi on the basis of extensive rock art and ancient [music] cultic remains found there. sites across the Gulf of Akaba in Saudi Arabia which have attracted a great deal of popular attention and considerable scholarly skepticism. Others argue for a location on the basis of readings of the biblical route [music] that would put it somewhere else entirely. There is no consensus. There is a monastery, a mountain, 3,700 steps [music] and 1,500 years of people climbing them with total conviction. I suspect some of you are going to tell me in the comments exactly which mountain is the real one. And I suspect no two of you will agree. That is sort of the point of this entry. From a place we cannot pin down to a place that handed us a name carved in stone. Number six, the step with a governor's name on it. For a very long time, there was an awkward gap in the record around Pontious Pilot. He appears in all four gospels. He appears in the Roman historian Tacitus and in the Jewish writers Josephus and Pho. But no physical object had been found from his own time and place that carried his name. Then in 1961, an Italian archaeological team was working at Cesaria Maritima, the great [music] harbor city on the coast of Israel that Herod the Great built and named for the emperor. They were excavating the Roman theater and they turned over a block of limestone that had been reused as part of a staircase. On its face was a partial Latin inscription. Damaged, incomplete, but readable. It named a Tiberium, a structure honoring the emperor Tiberius, and it named the man who dedicated it, Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judea. It is a plain unglamorous slab of stone and it is the first known inscription from his own province in his own lifetime bearing his name and his title. What gets me is the story of the stone itself. This was a dedication meant to be seen, meant to last, put up by the most powerful Roman official in the province. And within a few hundred years, somebody looking for building material picked it up, turned it over, and used it as a step. Thousands of people walked on the name of Pontious Pilot on their way to watch a show and not one of them thought anything of it. Cesaria was built to impress. Our next site was built to survive and it has been fought over more times than almost anywhere on Earth. Number five, the hill with the name everyone knows. In northern Israel, overlooking the Jezrael Valley, there is an artificial mound called Telmgiddo. From a distance, it looks like a low, flat hill with a good view. That view is the entire reason for everything that happened here. Megiddo sits above the pass where the main ancient road between Egypt and Mesopotamia squeezes through the hills. [music] If you held Megiddo, you controlled the road. So for thousands of years, everyone tried to hold Megiddo. Archaeologists have counted somewhere in the region of 20 separate layers of settlement stacked on top of each other here. city built on the ruins of city going back to the Bronze Age. There are gates, palaces, stables or storehouses depending on which archaeologist you ask, and an extraordinary water system, a deep shaft and tunnel cut through rock so the city could reach a spring outside the walls without ever opening the gate. You can walk [music] down it today. One of the earliest battles in recorded human history was fought here when the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmos III took the city and his scribes wrote the account down in detail. And then there is the name. In Hebrew, the mountain of Megiddo is Har Megiddo. Say that out loud a few times and let it slide through Greek transliteration and you get the word used in the book of Revelation for the site of the final battle. Armageddon. It is a real hill. There is a visitor center and [music] a car park. School groups eat their lunch up there in the wind, looking out over a very quiet green valley that has been the most fought over piece of farmland in the region for 3,000 years. That was a city that dug for water in secret. Our next entry is the tunnel where that idea was taken to its absolute limit. Number four, the tunnel two teams dug from opposite ends. Jerusalem has a problem that has shaped its entire history. The city sits on a defensible ridge, but its main water source, the Guihon spring, sits outside the walls down the slope in a siege that is fatal. The Bible records that [music] King Hezekiah facing the Assyrian Empire solved it. 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles describe him stopping up the spring and bringing the water inside the city. The tunnel is there. You can walk it. It runs roughly 533 m through solid [music] bedrock from the Guihan spring to the pool of Salom inside the ancient city. It is narrow in places you have to turn sideways. The ceiling is low enough in stretches that you go through hunched and there is water in it, cold and clear, running around your legs the whole way because the tunnel still does its job. In 1880, a boy waiting in the tunnel found something carved into the wall near the southern end. It was an inscription in ancient Hebrew script, and when it was read, it turned out to be an account written by the [music] workers themselves. It describes the moment of breakthrough, two teams cutting toward each other from opposite ends, the point where they could hear the voices of the other team through the rock, and then the axes meeting and the water flowing through to the pool. It is a construction crew almost 3,000 years ago writing down the best day of their working lives. And here is what nobody has [music] fully settled. The tunnel does not run straight. It curves in a long S shape and it is considerably longer than the direct distance between the two points. How two teams cutting blind through solid rock with hand tools following a bending path managed to meet each other at all is still argued over. Theories involve following a natural fissure or acoustic signaling or surveying from the surface. The inscription tells us the moment it happened. It does not tell us how they pulled it off. That tunnel emptied into a pool. Hold on to that because we are coming back to it. First, the oldest walled town on Earth. Number three, the city with the argument built into it. Jericho near the Jordan River is one of the oldest continuously inhabited places on the planet. Excavations at Tel Sultan have gone down through layer after layer, reaching settlement that goes back something like 11,000 years. At the bottom of that stack is a structure that stops people cold. A stone tower roughly 8 m tall with an internal staircase built around 8,000 years before Christ. That is thousands of years before writing, thousands of years before the pyramids. People with stone tools built a tower with a staircase inside it. And we still argue about what it was for. But of course, [music] that is not why most people know the name. Jericho is famous for the account in the book of Joshua where the Israelites circle the city and the walls come down. It is one of the most vivid images in the entire Bible. And the archaeology of that specific event has been fought over for a century. In the 1930s, John Garstang excavated here and concluded he had found collapsed walls matching the biblical account. Then in the 1950s, the British archaeologist Kathleen Kenyon returned with more rigorous stratographic methods and reached a very different conclusion. In her reading, the fortified city had been destroyed considerably earlier than the traditional date for Joshua, and at the relevant period, the site was largely unoccupied. Her work was widely accepted, and it remains the mainstream position. Other scholars have challenged the dating since, arguing for revised chronologies or reinterpretations of the pottery evidence, and the debate has never [music] fully closed. What is not in dispute is what you can see. There are walls at Jericho. There is a tower older than almost anything humans have built. There are burned layers in the earth from cities that ended violently. What those specific stones prove and about which century [music] is exactly the kind of question that fills a comment section. I am not going to pretend there is a settled answer because there is not. Go ahead and make your case below. from the oldest walls in the world to a place that was found by complete accident less than 25 years ago. Number two, the pool that turned up during a sewer repair. In 2004, workers in the city of David area of Jerusalem were carrying out repairs on a damaged sewage pipe. Ordinary municipal work, a digger scraping through the dirt, and the bucket came up with cut stone steps. Work stopped. Archaeologists Ronnie Reich and Eli Shukrron were brought in and what began to emerge was a monumental pool with broad stone steps descending into it dating to the second temple period. Coins found in the plaster helped date it. This is the pool of Silomme. It is the pool named in the Gospel of John where a man born blind is sent to wash. It is the pool that Hezekiah's tunnel from a moment ago was built to fill. And for most of 2,000 years, nobody knew exactly where it was. There was a smaller Byzantine era pool nearby that had long been shown to pilgrims. The actual pool from the first century was underneath a garden under layers of earth a few meters [music] from where people had been standing and pointing at the wrong thing for centuries. For years, only a portion of it could be uncovered because the land above it was privately owned by the Greek Orthodox Church and access was limited. Excavation has continued and expanded since, and plans have been announced to open the full pool to the public. What I keep [music] coming back to is how close it was the whole time. Not lost in a desert, not buried under a mountain, under a vegetable garden, [music] in a city where thousands of people walk past every single day waiting for a pipe to break. And that brings us to number one, because the greatest discovery on this list also happened by accident, and it happened because somebody was bored. Number one, the caves above the Dead Sea. In 1947, a young Bedawin shepherd named Muhammad Edib was looking after goats in the dry cliffs above the northwestern shore of the Dead Sea near a place called Kumran. The most repeated version of the story is that he threw a stone into a cave opening, either to scare an animal out or just out of idleness and heard the sound of pottery breaking. Inside were tall clay [music] jars. And inside some of the jars were scrolls wrapped in linen, dry as paper, preserved by one of the harshest and most arid climates on earth. Nobody involved understood at first what they had. The first scrolls passed through dealers in Bethlehem and were sold for very little. It took time and the involvement of scholars and institutions before the world grasped it. Over the following decade, searching intensified. In the end, around 11 caves in the cliffs around Kuman gave up fragments of somewhere in the region of 900 separate manuscripts. Among them was a nearly complete copy of the book of Isaiah. Before that scroll, the oldest complete Hebrew manuscripts of the biblical text [music] available to scholars dated from around the 10th century after Christ. The Isaiah scroll from Kuman was roughly a thousand years older. A thousand years of copying by hand by generations of scribes suddenly opened [music] up for direct comparison. And when scholars compared them, the text turned out to be remarkably consistent with variations that were mostly minor. That single fact reshaped the entire academic conversation about how the text had been transmitted. The caves also held things nobody expected. community rules for [music] the group that apparently lived at the settlement nearby. Hymns, commentaries, calendars, texts that never made it into any Bible, and one object that is unlike everything else in the collection. In one cave, they found a scroll that is not written on parchment or papyrus. It is beaten copper, and it does not contain scripture. It contains [music] a list. The copper scroll describes locations, dozens of them, and quantities of gold and silver said to be hidden at each one. It reads like an inventory under a certain set of steps in a sistern beneath a tomb. Numbers, weights, directions. Scholars disagree sharply about it. Some think it records the real treasure of the temple hidden before the Roman destruction. Others think it is a folk tradition, a legend written down, or a list of things intended rather than things done. People have gone looking. Expeditions have hunted for the sites described in it since it was first translated in the 1950s. As far as anyone has been able to confirm, not a single one of the caches listed on that scroll has ever been found. Every place on this list started as a name in a text. a city, a mountain, a well, a pool, and one by one, a shepherd stone, a broken sewage pipe, a team of demining engineers, and a looters tunnel turn those names into places with car parks and admission times where you can stand on the ground and look at the same view. What I find remarkable is how ordinary the moment of discovery usually was. Somebody fixing a pipe, a boy waiting in cold water in a tunnel, a bored teenager throwing a rock into a hole in a cliff. Nobody in any of those stories woke up planning to change what the world knew. If you made it all the way here, tell me in the comments which of these you would actually go and stand in tomorrow if someone handed you the ticket. And you pick where we go next. cities that were swallowed by the sea or the deepest places on earth that nobody has ever reached the bottom of. Say the word below.
